title: Month-over-month change

WITH m AS (
    SELECT DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(OrderDate), MONTH(OrderDate), 1) AS MonthStart,
           SUM(OrderTotal) AS Total

    GROUP BY DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(OrderDate), MONTH(OrderDate), 1)

       LAG(Total) OVER (ORDER BY MonthStart)         AS PrevMonth,
       Total - LAG(Total) OVER (ORDER BY MonthStart) AS Change

    SELECT p.Region, p.CustomerName, SUM(e.OrderTotal) AS TotalOrderTotal,

    GROUP BY p.Region, p.CustomerID, p.CustomerName
)
SELECT Region, CustomerName, TotalOrderTotal
FROM t
WHERE rn <= 3
ORDER BY Region, rn;

title: Repeat orders within N days
q: Find orders that happened within @Days days of the same customer's previous order. Use @Days = 145. Show customer, previous date, current date and gap.
sql:
DECLARE @Days int = 145;

WITH v AS (
    SELECT CustomerID, OrderID, OrderDate,
           LAG(OrderDate) OVER (PARTITION BY CustomerID ORDER BY OrderDate, OrderID) AS PrevDate
    FROM ecommerce.Orders
)
SELECT CustomerID, PrevDate, OrderDate,
       DATEDIFF(day, PrevDate, OrderDate) AS GapDays
FROM v
WHERE PrevDate IS NOT NULL
  AND DATEDIFF(day, PrevDate, OrderDate) <= @Days
ORDER BY CustomerID, OrderDate;

title: Constraint vs trigger vs app
q: Write a query that shows, for each table, how many PK, FK, UNIQUE, CHECK and DEFAULT constraints it has.
sql:
SELECT OBJECT_NAME(parent_object_id) AS TableName,
       SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'PK' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS PK,
       SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'F'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS FK,
       SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'UQ' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS UQ,
       SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'C'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS CK,
       SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'D'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS DF
FROM sys.objects
WHERE type IN ('PK', 'F', 'UQ', 'C', 'D')
  AND SCHEMA_NAME(schema_id) = 'ecommerce'
GROUP BY parent_object_id
ORDER BY TableName;
how: Prefer declarative constraints: they are faster, always applied, and help the optimizer. Use triggers only for cross-table rules, and application checks for friendly messages.

title: Order chain for one customer
q: Starting from customer 1's first order, use a recursive CTE to walk forward through that customer's orders in date order, with a step number.

WITH Ordered AS (
    SELECT OrderID, OrderDate,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY OrderDate, OrderID) AS rn
    FROM ecommerce.Orders
    WHERE CustomerID = 1
), Chain AS (
    SELECT OrderID, OrderDate, rn, 0 AS Step
    FROM Ordered
    WHERE rn = 1

    SELECT o.OrderID, o.OrderDate, o.rn, c.Step + 1

)

title: MAXRECURSION
q: Generate numbers 1 to 200 with a recursive CTE. (The default limit is 100 levels.)
sql:
WITH N AS (
    SELECT 1 AS n
    UNION ALL
    SELECT n + 1 FROM N WHERE n < 200
)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS HowMany, MAX(n) AS LastNumber
FROM N
OPTION (MAXRECURSION 200);

title: Top 3 products by spend per region

title: Month-over-month with a calendar
q: For all 12 months of 2024 (even empty ones), show total order total, previous month's total and growth %.

WITH Months AS (
    SELECT CAST('2024-01-01' AS date) AS m
    UNION ALL
    SELECT DATEADD(month, 1, m) FROM Months WHERE m < '2024-12-01'
), Totals AS (
    SELECT mo.m, ISNULL(SUM(e.OrderTotal), 0) AS Total
    FROM Months AS mo
    LEFT JOIN ecommerce.Orders AS e
           ON e.OrderDate >= mo.m AND e.OrderDate < DATEADD(month, 1, mo.m)
    GROUP BY mo.m
)
SELECT m AS MonthStart, Total,
       LAG(Total) OVER (ORDER BY m) AS PrevTotal,
       CAST(100.0 * (Total - LAG(Total) OVER (ORDER BY m))

title: Org-chart style hierarchy with path
q: Build a small hierarchy in a table variable (region head > team > customer) and list it with a recursive CTE, showing each level and a path like Head > North > Olivia.

DECLARE @Org TABLE (NodeID int, ParentID int NULL, NodeName nvarchar(100));
INSERT INTO @Org VALUES (0, NULL, N'Head');
INSERT INTO @Org
SELECT DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Region), 0, Region
FROM ecommerce.Customers
GROUP BY Region;
INSERT INTO @Org
SELECT 100 + p.CustomerID, r.NodeID, p.CustomerName
FROM ecommerce.Customers AS p
JOIN @Org AS r ON r.NodeName = p.Region
WHERE p.CustomerID <= 6;

WITH Tree AS (
    SELECT NodeID, NodeName, 0 AS Lvl, CAST(NodeName AS nvarchar(400)) AS PathText
    FROM @Org
    WHERE ParentID IS NULL
    UNION ALL
    SELECT o.NodeID, o.NodeName, t.Lvl + 1,
           CAST(t.PathText + N' > ' + o.NodeName AS nvarchar(400))
    FROM @Org AS o
    JOIN Tree AS t ON o.ParentID = t.NodeID
)
SELECT NodeID, Lvl, PathText
FROM Tree
ORDER BY PathText;

title: Age in years done right

       DATEDIFF(year, @Born, d.AsOf)
         - CASE WHEN DATEADD(year, DATEDIFF(year, @Born, d.AsOf), @Born) > d.AsOf
                THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS AgeYears,

title: MERGE: sync a staging table
q: Sync product prices from a staging list: update prices that changed, insert new products, and report each action.
sql:
DECLARE @Stage TABLE (ProductID int, ProductName nvarchar(80), SKU varchar(20), UnitPrice decimal(12,2));
INSERT INTO @Stage VALUES
    (1,  N'Acetaminophen 325mg tablet', 'EB-00001', 0.09),   -- price change
    (2,  N'Acetaminophen 500mg tablet', 'EB-00002', 0.10),   -- no change
    (51, N'Loratadine 10mg tablet',     'EB-00051', 0.12);   -- new

MERGE ecommerce.Products AS t
USING @Stage AS s
   ON t.ProductID = s.ProductID
WHEN MATCHED AND t.UnitPrice <> s.UnitPrice THEN
    UPDATE SET t.UnitPrice = s.UnitPrice
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET THEN
    INSERT (ProductID, ProductName, SKU, UnitPrice)
    VALUES (s.ProductID, s.ProductName, s.SKU, s.UnitPrice)
OUTPUT $action AS ActionTaken, inserted.ProductID, deleted.UnitPrice AS OldCost, inserted.UnitPrice AS NewCost;
how: MERGE does insert, update and (optionally) delete in one statement. The extra `AND t.UnitPrice <> s.UnitPrice` skips rows that did not change. $action in OUTPUT reports what happened to each row. MERGE must end with a semicolon.

title: Isolation levels
q: Name SQL Server's transaction isolation levels and the problem each one prevents. Show the current level.
sql:
SELECT CASE transaction_isolation_level
         WHEN 1 THEN 'READ UNCOMMITTED' WHEN 2 THEN 'READ COMMITTED'
         WHEN 3 THEN 'REPEATABLE READ'  WHEN 4 THEN 'SERIALIZABLE'
         WHEN 5 THEN 'SNAPSHOT' END AS IsolationLevel
FROM sys.dm_exec_sessions
WHERE session_id = @@SPID;
how: READ UNCOMMITTED allows dirty reads. READ COMMITTED (the default) prevents dirty reads. REPEATABLE READ also prevents non-repeatable reads. SERIALIZABLE also prevents phantom rows. title: Self join: next order

title: Joins that multiply rows
q: Show each customer's total order order total and total number of order items. Make sure the order total is not double counted.
sql:
SELECT p.CustomerID, p.CustomerName,
       ISNULL(ch.TotalOrderTotal, 0) AS TotalOrderTotal,
       ISNULL(li.OrderItems, 0) AS OrderItems
FROM ecommerce.Customers AS p
LEFT JOIN (SELECT CustomerID, SUM(OrderTotal) AS TotalOrderTotal
           FROM ecommerce.Orders
           GROUP BY CustomerID) AS ch ON ch.CustomerID = p.CustomerID
LEFT JOIN (SELECT e.CustomerID, COUNT(*) AS OrderItems
           FROM ecommerce.OrderItems AS r
           JOIN ecommerce.Orders AS e ON e.OrderID = r.OrderID
           GROUP BY e.CustomerID) AS li ON li.CustomerID = p.CustomerID
ORDER BY TotalOrderTotal DESC;
how: If you join Orders and OrderItems first and then SUM(OrderTotal), an order with 2 order items has its order total counted twice (fan-out). Aggregating each child table separately before joining fixes this. Interviewers often test whether you spot fan-out.

title: Short-circuit is not guaranteed
q: Return products where the name has a space and the text before the first space is longer than 8 characters. Write it safely so CHARINDEX never gives a negative length.
sql:
SELECT ProductName
FROM ecommerce.Products
WHERE CASE WHEN CHARINDEX(' ', ProductName) > 0
           THEN LEN(LEFT(ProductName, CHARINDEX(' ', ProductName) - 1))
           ELSE 0
      END > 8;
how: SQL Server does not promise to evaluate AND conditions left to right, so `CHARINDEX(...) > 0 AND LEN(LEFT(... - 1)) > 8` could still error on a row with no space. A CASE expression controls the order. This is a senior-level detail.

title: STRING_AGG

title: NOT IN and the NULL trap
q: Interview trap: show why NOT IN fails when the list contains NULL. Find orders that are not a parent of any other order, first with NOT IN (wrong), then with NOT EXISTS (right).
sql:
SELECT
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ecommerce.Orders AS e
   WHERE e.OrderID NOT IN (SELECT ParentOrderID
                               FROM ecommerce.Orders)) AS NotIn_Wrong,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ecommerce.Orders AS e
   WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ecommerce.Orders AS c
                     WHERE c.ParentOrderID = e.OrderID)) AS NotExists_Right;
how: ParentOrderID is NULL on every row here. `x NOT IN (..., NULL)` is never true, so NOT IN returns 0. NOT EXISTS ignores the NULLs and correctly finds that no order is a parent. You can also fix NOT IN by adding `WHERE ParentOrderID IS NOT NULL` inside the subquery.

title: Orders after a customer's first order item
q: For each customer who has an order item, count how many of their orders happened after the order of their first order item.
sql:
SELECT x.CustomerID, COUNT(e.OrderID) AS LaterOrders
FROM (SELECT e1.CustomerID, MIN(e1.OrderDate) AS FirstRxDate
      FROM ecommerce.OrderItems AS li
      JOIN ecommerce.Orders AS e1 ON e1.OrderID = li.OrderID
      GROUP BY e1.CustomerID) AS x
LEFT JOIN ecommerce.Orders AS e
       ON e.CustomerID = x.CustomerID
      AND e.OrderDate > x.FirstRxDate
GROUP BY x.CustomerID
ORDER BY LaterOrders DESC, x.CustomerID;
how: The derived table finds each customer's first order item date. The LEFT JOIN on a date condition counts the later orders, and customers with none get 0.

title: IN vs EXISTS vs JOIN
q: Return customers with at least one Pending order three ways (IN, EXISTS, JOIN with DISTINCT). Each should return the same count.
sql:
SELECT
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ecommerce.Customers
   WHERE CustomerID IN (SELECT CustomerID FROM ecommerce.Orders
                       WHERE OrderStatus = 'Pending')) AS ViaIn,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ecommerce.Customers AS p
   WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ecommerce.Orders AS e
                 WHERE e.CustomerID = p.CustomerID AND e.OrderStatus = 'Pending')) AS ViaExists,
  (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT p.CustomerID)
   FROM ecommerce.Customers AS p
   JOIN ecommerce.Orders AS e ON e.CustomerID = p.CustomerID
   WHERE e.OrderStatus = 'Pending') AS ViaJoin;
how: All three give the same answer. A plain JOIN repeats a customer for each matching order, which is why DISTINCT is needed. IN and EXISTS never duplicate rows.

title: Products priced above their group's average
q: Products come in families (the first word of the name, e.g. 'Ibuprofen'). List products that cost more than the average of their own family.
sql:
SELECT m.ProductName, m.UnitPrice
FROM ecommerce.Products AS m
WHERE m.UnitPrice > (SELECT AVG(x.UnitPrice)
                    FROM ecommerce.Products AS x
                    WHERE LEFT(x.ProductName, CHARINDEX(' ', x.ProductName) - 1)
                        = LEFT(m.ProductName, CHARINDEX(' ', m.ProductName) - 1))
ORDER BY m.ProductName;
how: The family is computed with LEFT + CHARINDEX (text before the first space). The correlated subquery averages only products of the same family.
